displayQuote: Thousands of candles can be lighted from a single candle, and the life of the candle will not be shortened. Happiness never decreases by being shared

meta.title: Who really said "Thousands of candles can be lighted from a single candle"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not in the Pali canon. The flame-sharing image is genuinely Buddhist — it appears in the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections and the Vimalakirti-nirdesa — but this English wording, including the 'happiness' sentence, comes from a modern Japanese anthology, The Teaching of Buddha.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Thousands of candles can be lighted from a single candle'?
meta.ogDescription: The one-lamp-lights-many image is real Buddhism. The candles, and the sentence about happiness, are a 20th-century anthology's phrasing — not a translation of anything the Buddha is recorded as saying.

answer.label: Not canonical — a modern anthology’s phrasing
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · modern Japanese Buddhist anthology, 20th century
answer.sourceLine: This wording appears in no Pali text — not the Dhammapada, not the Nikayas. What is genuine is the image: a flame passed from one lamp to many without diminishing the first turns up in the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections (section 10) and, in Mahayana literature, in the Vimalakirti-nirdesa. The candle version circulating in English — and especially the closing sentence about happiness, which has no scriptural counterpart at all — traces to The Teaching of Buddha, the anthology of sutra paraphrase and commentary published by Bukkyo Dendo Kyokai of Japan and left in hotel drawers across Asia. Buddhist in sentiment; not a quotation.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Not present — no Dhammapada or Nikaya verse
Vimalakirti-nirdesa — one lamp lighting hundreds of thousands
The Teaching of Buddha, Bukkyo Dendo Kyokai (Japan)

source.excerpt: It is like a lighted torch whose flame can be distributed to ever so many other torches which people may bring along; and therewith they will cook food and dispel darkness, while the original torch itself remains burning ever the same.
trail: First test: does it appear in the Pali canon? No. The Dhammapada has no candle verse, and no Nikaya discourse contains this sentence in any translation we could locate. The line fails the standard test outright the investigation ↗.

Second test: is the idea canonical? Yes, and that is what makes this one interesting. The Sutra of Forty-Two Sections, a very early Chinese Buddhist text, gives the torch passage quoted above; the Mahayana Vimalakirti-nirdesa has a single lamp kindling hundreds of thousands of lamps without being diminished. Neither is Pali, and in the Vimalakirti the speaker is Vimalakirti, not the Buddha.

Third test: where did the English come from? The candle wording, complete with the ‘happiness never decreases by being shared’ coda, is carried by The Teaching of Buddha, the Bukkyo Dendo Kyokai anthology — a book that mixes translated sutra material with modern explanatory prose and does not always mark where one stops and the other starts. That is precisely the seam a quotation slips through.
source.excerptNote: The genuine ancestor, in an early English translation. Notice what it is actually about: it is an argument that giving teaching away costs the teacher nothing, made with cooking and darkness rather than with happiness. The sentimental turn — happiness as the thing being shared — is the modern addition, and it is the part everyone quotes.

sourceLink.text: Fake Buddha Quotes — tracing the candles

source.rightsNote: Rights here are unresolved and worth care. The underlying sutras are ancient and unprotectable, but you never reproduce a sutra — you reproduce somebody’s translation, and a translation carries its own copyright. The torch passage above appears to come from an early-twentieth-century English rendering, which would put it in the public domain in most places, but we could not establish the translator or year and so we do not assert it. The candle wording is worse: it comes from a modern anthology, The Teaching of Buddha, whose text is in copyright to its Japanese publisher. Quote the candles as a modern paraphrase with attribution; do not treat them as free ancient scripture. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Gautama Buddha
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on the Buddha
author.metaLine: c. 5th century BCE · founder of Buddhism · northern India
author.bio: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught in northern India in roughly the fifth century BCE, and his discourses were carried orally for centuries before being written down in Pali. That oral gap is exactly why his name attracts lines like this one: a tradition with no signed manuscripts and a genuine fondness for lamp-and-flame imagery makes it very easy for a warm modern sentence to sound like scripture. He is also, in most Western bookshops, represented less by the Nikayas than by anthologies — and anthologies are where paraphrase and translation get quietly mixed.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is the hard case, and the honest verdict has two halves. The sentiment is genuinely Buddhist and has real textual ancestors. The sentence is not something the Buddha is recorded as saying.

items.why: The standard test for a Buddha quotation is whether it appears in the Dhammapada or the Nikayas. This does not, in any wording. You can check the first of those yourself in the public-domain 1881 translation.

Section 10 gives the torch whose flame lights many torches without being spent — and applies it to giving away teaching, not happiness. It is also a Chinese text, not Pali, so it is at one further remove from the historical Buddha than most readers assume about the sutra ↗.

The Vimalakirti-nirdesa has the one-lamp-lights-hundreds-of-thousands passage, but it belongs to Vimalakirti, a layman, and it is about establishing beings in enlightenment. Quoting it as the Buddha misidentifies the speaker as well as the subject.
‘Happiness never decreases by being shared’ is the line people actually want, and it is the one part with no ancient parallel anywhere. It is modern anthology prose the trace ↗.

Both forms circulate widely, which is itself a tell: a translated scriptural verse tends to travel with its translator’s wording intact, while an anthology paraphrase drifts freely as people retype it.

misattribution.truthLine: Not canonical. The flame image is real Buddhism — Sutra of Forty-Two Sections, section 10, and the Vimalakirti-nirdesa — but the candles, and the sentence about happiness, are modern the trace ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is a rare thing: a piece of moral advice with a physical demonstration built in. You can actually light a candle from a candle and watch nothing be lost, which makes the claim about happiness feel less like a wish and more like a fact about the world.

It also flatters the person quoting it. Generosity that costs nothing is the easiest generosity to recommend — which may be why the ancient version, about handing on teaching to people who need it, has been quietly replaced by a version about feeling good.
context.detailsSummary: Not canonical is not the same as not Buddhist
detailsBody: A line can express real Buddhist teaching and still not be a quotation. This is one of those.
The flame-passed-on image is old, widespread and doctrinally serious — it is how Buddhist texts talk about transmission.
What is modern is the English sentence, the candles in place of torches, and the substitution of happiness for teaching.
The practical consequence: put it on a slide as ‘a Buddhist saying’ and you are on solid ground. Put ‘—Buddha’ underneath it and you are inventing a citation.
context.pull: The torch was about giving away teaching. The candle is about feeling good.
